newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore oil trader eyes China diesel market.
newsitem.headline: Singapore oil trader eyes China diesel market.

text.p: An independent Singapore oil trader is seeking to capture a big share of the lucrative Chinese diesel market with its massive purchases, industry sources said on Friday.

Some traders viewed this positively, saying that by raising its profile the trader, Hin Leong Trading, was allowing traditional sellers such as major oil companies to avoid the risk of having their sales reneged on by Chinese end-users.

"With China having a history of reneging on their deals when prices turned against their favour, oil companies, including majors are more than happy to sell oil to Hin Leong and let them undertake the financial risks involving letter of credits, logistic and operational risks," a trader in Singapore said.
However, sources at major oil companies in Hong Kong said Hin Leong has not taken over their market share in China, citing continued stable diesel exports to the mainland.
But oil majors in Hong Kong may have failed to expand their market share in line with growing diesel demand in China. That increased demand had been captured by Hin Leong, traders in Singapore said.
Hin Leong officials declined to comment.
In January, end-users in China refused to accept up to 400,000 tonnes of diesel when international spot prices plunged after Chinese importers had earlier bought the cargoes at much higher prices.
Hin Leong, its sister company Sanko and Japanese trader Marubeni International Petroleum Co have bought around 17 million barrels since March 3 worth about US$500 million.
On Thursday, Hin Leong and the two traders chalked another one-day record purchase of 2.44 million barrels from a cross section of sellers, many of whom were active sellers to China.
Traders noted that China has not been visible in its diesel purchases since February, triggering concerns that Hin Leong and the other buyers would not be able to sell their cargoes.
They feared the unplaced diesel might eventually find its way back to the regional market and lead to a price collapse.

But data released by Chinese customs on Friday showed that China imported 793,252 tonnes of diesel in March, taking its tally for the year to 2.06 million tonnes (15 million barrels). In 1996 China imported 4.6 million tonnes of diesel.
Traders noted the volume showed China had not stopped importing as the market thought.
The massive purchases have triggered the largest-ever flow of diesel from the West to East Asia and India totalling more than 15 million barrels.
"Most of the oil would go to China or to buyers who are short into India," a trader close to Hin Leong said.
The source said Hin Leong was able to absorb the cargoes from the West as there is real demand in East Asia ahead of the peak refinery maintenance season in May and June.
They said refinery shutdowns in South Korea, Japan and China would cause most Chinese buyers to look south for imports.
Some traders said Hin Leong was able to capture an increasing slice of the Chinese market as it offered attractive terms for diesel sales to China buyers.
Some traders said Hin Leong might also be hedging the price risks on behalf of Chinese end-users. But a Hin Leong trader declined to comment on this.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3082)
